snippets.output: Given the patient's presentation, laboratory results, and clinical course, the most appropriate next step in management is to repeat the urinalysis. The presence of 3+ proteinuria on urinalysis warrants further evaluation to confirm its presence and assess whether it is persistent or transient.

Proteinuria can be a significant indicator of renal disease. The presence of 3+ proteinuria on urinalysis, with an otherwise unremarkable physical examination and no signs or symptoms of renal disease, suggests the need for further investigation to rule out renal disease.
A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast is not indicated in this case, as there is no indication of acute abdominal pathology or suspected obstruction.
A renal biopsy is not indicated in this case because the proteinuria is not severe, and there is no indication of renal failure or chronic kidney disease.
Urine dipstick in the morning and in the afternoon is not the most appropriate next step in management, as the patient has already had a urinalysis with noted proteinuria.

Urine electrolytes and creatinine may be useful in certain cases of renal disease, but it is not the most appropriate next step in management in this case. There is no indication of electrolyte imbalances or renal failure.
